⚙️ Controls
Volume: 5.0 L
Pressure: 1.00 atm
Temperature: 298 K (Constant)
PV = 5.00 atm·L
Average Kinetic Energy: 6.17e-21 J

Rotate and zoom the scene with mouse or touch.
Adjust the slider to see effects on gas pressure and volume.
Observe the relationship between pressure and volume.
Note: Temperature (and thus particle speed) remains constant in this isothermal process.

Welcome to our interactive Boyle's Law demonstration! Boyle's Law, formulated by Robert Boyle in 1662, is one of the fundamental gas laws in physics. It states that at constant temperature, the pressure of a given mass of gas is inversely proportional to its volume. Mathematically, this is expressed as: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ = constant In this simulation, you'll observe: 1. A sealed container with gas particles 2. A movable piston that changes the volume 3. Real-time pressure and volume measurements 4. The constant product of pressure and volume (PV) 5. Particle behavior at microscopic and macroscopic levels Key concepts to observe: • As volume decreases, pressure increases • As volume increases, pressure decreases • The product of pressure and volume remains constant • Particle speed remains constant (isothermal process) • Collision frequency changes with volume Use the controls to: • Move the piston up and down • Switch between macroscopic and microscopic views • Observe the pressure-volume relationship • Verify the constant PV product This demonstration helps visualize the kinetic theory of gases and the relationship between pressure and volume in an isothermal process.

Electrostatics: 3D Electric Field Visualization
Electric Charge

A fundamental property of matter, just like mass. It's what makes particles attract or repel each other through electromagnetic forces.

Elementary Charge (e): 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
• Smallest amount of charge that can exist freely
• Electron: -e charge
• Proton: +e charge
Coulomb's Law

F = k(q₁q₂)/r²

Force between charges:
• Opposite charges attract (green arrows)
• Like charges repel (red arrows)
• Force decreases with distance (1/r²)
• k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N⋅m²/C²
  • Red sphere: Positive charge (+q)
  • Blue sphere: Negative charge (−q)
  • Arrows: Electric field direction & intensity
  • Curves: Electric field lines (animated)
  • Force vectors: Green (attraction) / Red (repulsion)
Modes: Single Charge & Dipole (toggle above)
Controls: Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, right-drag to pan
Interactive: Drag charges to move them, use sliders to change charge values
Physics: Field lines point away from +q and toward −q. Field strength shown by arrow length.
For ICSE Class 11/12 Physics

Real-World Applications

Water Molecules

Water's dipole nature enables it to dissolve many substances

Ionic Bonds

How opposite charges attract to form stable compounds

Capacitors

Storing energy using separated charges

Lightning

Natural discharge of accumulated charges
